title: B2B Product-Led Growth, Funnels, and Reverse Trials
content:
Lenny Rachitsky: Welcome Elena Verna. Elena is one of the most sought-after growth advisors in tech, having advised companies like Miro, Amplitude, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey, and Netlify. Elena, everyone is talking about PLG (Product-Led Growth). How do you define modern B2B PLG?

Elena Verna: PLG is not a go-to-market strategy in isolation; it is an organizational distribution philosophy. In traditional enterprise sales-led growth, the product is hidden behind a demo form, an SDR qualifying call, and a procurement cycle. In Product-Led Growth, the product itself is the primary vehicle for acquisition, retention, monetization, and expansion. The end-user is empowered to experience value before any contract is signed.

Lenny Rachitsky: What is the single biggest mistake companies make when attempting to transition from sales-led to product-led?

Elena Verna: They slap a free trial button on their website and call it PLG. That fails 99% of the time. The biggest mistake is confusing 'User Onboarding' with 'Setup'. Most SaaS products make you invite 5 colleagues, configure your CRM API, and set up your billing profile before you ever see value. True PLG requires shortening the Time-to-Value (TTV) to under 3 minutes. The user must experience the 'Aha Moment'—the realization of core product value—in their first session.

Lenny Rachitsky: What is your current thesis on Freemium vs Free Trial vs Reverse Trial?

Elena Verna: I am a massive advocate of the Reverse Trial. In a standard free trial, the user gets all enterprise features for 14 days, and when it expires, they hit a paywall and leave. In a reverse trial, you give them all premium features for 14 days. If they don't upgrade, you don't lock them out; you gracefully downgrade them to a functional free tier. This preserves your retention loop. The user continues getting value, stays active, and when their team expands or hit usage limits, they upgrade. It combines the acquisition power of freemium with the urgency of a trial.
